sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Cursor Says Stolen Fireworks AI Key Led to Trojanized Claude Code Extension Incident

stories.headline: Cursor traces Claude Code extension hijack to stolen Fireworks AI key
stories.dek: An access key exposed in the Fireworks AI breach let an attacker reach Cursor's systems and push a backdoored extension to up to 5,000 users.
stories.body:
The trojanized Claude Code extension that appeared on Cursor's extension marketplace started with someone else's breach. In a Friday update, Cursor said an attacker obtained an access key it had issued to Fireworks AI, an inference provider it used, after the key was exposed in a breach at Fireworks, The Hacker News reports.

"The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them," Cursor said. That bucket held limited coding agent traces from sessions not in Privacy Mode, most dating back to 2025 and cleared for model training. Some traces contained credentials that had never been scrubbed, exposing API credentials for less than 0.01 percent of customers.

The attacker used those credentials to reach some of Cursor's SaaS tools. From there they accessed archived non-production source code repositories, limited customer support data and emails, product usage metrics and contact details, summaries of some agent conversations, and credentials users had sent to Cursor support. Cursor says it revoked and rotated credentials and temporarily disabled internal and product services, which disrupted some features.

On October 29, the attacker used a stolen internal credential to plant trojanized versions of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension directly in the cache serving Cursor's marketplace. The malicious build tried to install a persistent SSH backdoor. Cursor says at most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions that day may have received it, and it stayed up for about 11 hours. Affected versions are 2.1.312 and 2.1.313. Cursor took the marketplace offline, notified affected users and says it has seen no further malicious activity since November 1.

Cursor has moved all inference traffic off Fireworks and cut its access to shared data sets. It says there is no evidence that Privacy Mode users, customer code repositories, its production environment, the Cursor app or other marketplace extensions were affected.

Fireworks' breach has spread beyond Cursor. Uber told California regulators that a service provider's compromised credentials were used to access Uber data, including thousands of drivers' license records. TechCrunch identified that provider as Fireworks AI. Notion also confirmed last week that its data was stolen in the Fireworks hack.
key_points: Key Cursor issued to Fireworks AI was exposed in the Fireworks breach
Unscrubbed credentials in agent traces let the attacker move deeper
Backdoored Claude Code versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 live about 11 hours
Uber and Notion also hit through the Fireworks AI breach
stories.why_it_matters: If you used Cursor without Privacy Mode, anything pasted into agent sessions, including secrets, may have ended up in training data shared with vendors. Anyone who installed Claude Code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from Cursor's marketplace on October 29 should treat that machine as compromised.

sources.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

stories.headline: Microsoft 365 outage silences pool alarm, 15 hotel guests hurt
stories.dek: An email-only warning at Phantasialand's Hotel Ling Bao never arrived as a faulty dosing system overloaded the pool with chlorine.
stories.body:
Fifteen guests at Phantasialand's Hotel Ling Bao in Brühl, Germany, were injured after a pool overdosed with chlorine, and the alarm never got through. WDR reports that the park told the broadcaster the maintenance safety system had raised the alarm by email, but Microsoft's outage on Friday meant the messages never arrived. A defective automatic dosing system had pumped too much chlorine into the pool.

Thirteen guests initially reported respiratory irritation, and the count later rose to 15. Four were taken to the hospital, with one kept for observation over a moderate injury, according to WDR. Tom's Hardware, citing Notebookcheck, says 40 first responders were deployed. The water was replaced and the pool has reopened.

Tom's Hardware says the Outlook outage ran from November 12 to 14 and argues that safety systems need local or analog backups.
key_points: A faulty dosing system overloaded a pool at Phantasialand's Hotel Ling Bao with chlorine, injuring 15 guests.
The safety system's email alarms failed to arrive during Microsoft's Outlook outage, the park told WDR.
Four guests were hospitalized and one was kept for observation.

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker

stories.headline: uBlock Origin flaw let websites inject code into any site
stories.dek: A researcher showed how a malicious page could drive the element picker to add trusted filters that run JavaScript anywhere. The bug is fixed.
stories.body:
A now-fixed universal XSS flaw in uBlock Origin let a malicious website trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters, according to a write-up on iter.ca. Because trusted filters can inject JavaScript, an attacker could run code in the context of any site after a single click. The main bug hit the MV2 Firefox version. A similar but less serious issue affected uBO Lite, the MV3 version.

The attack embedded uBO's element picker in an invisible iframe, sent it messages to stage a filter, then lured the user into clicking a hidden Create button. Smuggling a newline into one field let it bypass the picker's filter restrictions.

The researcher says GPT-5.6 Sol found the issue and Claude wrote most of the proof-of-concept code. The story drew 224 points on Hacker News.
key_points: A malicious site could make uBlock Origin add trusted filters that run JavaScript on any domain with one click.
The flaw abused the element picker via an invisible iframe and spoofed messages; it is now fixed.
The researcher credits GPT-5.6 Sol with finding the bug and Claude with writing most of the proof of concept.

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: Two HPE Juniper network routers grounded all US flights on Friday

stories.headline: FAA traces Friday's nationwide ground stop to two Juniper routers
stories.dek: New HPE Juniper routers in Arkansas and Texas flooded the FAA's aging copper network, cutting off controllers from pilots for about four hours.
stories.body:
Two newly installed HPE Juniper routers triggered Friday night's nationwide US ground stop, Tom's Hardware reports, citing the Wall Street Journal and FAA statements. Routers at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, began sending a high volume of data across the agency's communications network. "A thousand connections over every four to five seconds," FAA technology chief Rebecca Guy said.

That load overwhelmed the FAA's decades-old copper network, disrupting contact between controllers and pilots. Trouble first surfaced at Indianapolis Center. FAA staff traced it to a specific router feature and disabled it on all Juniper routers. Restoring communications took about four hours.

HPE says the routers worked as intended and "did not fail." FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency is investigating whether installation, configuration or the hardware itself was at fault. It is only the third nationwide ground stop, after 9/11 and the 2023 NOTAM outage.
key_points: New Juniper routers in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas, flooded the FAA network; staff disabled the responsible feature on all Juniper routers.
The FAA's aging copper network buckled; communications took about four hours to restore.
HPE says the routers "did not fail"; the FAA is investigating installation, configuration and hardware.

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge

stories.headline: Judge lets DRAM price-fixing suit against Micron, Samsung, SK hynix proceed
stories.dek: Judge Noël Wise found collusion claims plausible after prices rose as much as 500 percent, likening the chipmakers to "hawks flying in formation."
stories.body:
A federal judge has denied a motion by Micron, Samsung and SK hynix to dismiss a proposed class action accusing them of colluding to restrict DRAM supply, Tom's Hardware reports. Judge Noël Wise rejected the companies' claim that the case is "a rerun" of a 2018 antitrust suit, citing new evidence. The firms argued they watch each other like hawks. Wise wrote that the allegations are "more akin to hawks flying in formation, an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do."

The 17 plaintiffs, individuals and small businesses, cite simultaneous production cuts from October 2022 to April 2023, a pivot to HBM, DDR4 wind-downs within three months, and no capacity expansion despite prices up as much as 500 percent in a year. The companies say the moves reflect independent self-interest. They must respond by December 7.
key_points: Judge Noël Wise denied Micron, Samsung and SK hynix's motion to dismiss a DRAM price-fixing class action.
Plaintiffs allege coordinated supply cuts amid a shortage that pushed prices up as much as 500 percent in one year.
The companies must respond by December 7, with a case management conference set for January 2027.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: FBI warns ARTEX AI hacking tool is powering global cyberattacks

stories.headline: FBI warns attackers are using ARTEX AI tool to automate breaches
stories.dek: The open-source framework drives LLM agents through intrusions and was tied to the ConnectWise supply-chain attack on Microsoft 365 tenants.
stories.body:
The FBI says multiple threat actors have weaponized ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration testing framework, since at least August 2026, BleepingComputer reports. A FLASH advisory released Friday says some intrusions went from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. Targets span the financial, government, technology, defense and healthcare sectors.

ARTEX is written in Go and plugs into external models including Claude, GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok and Kimi. Its agents handle reconnaissance, exploitation, privilege escalation and data theft. Its developer pulled the GitHub repository on October 8, but forks, archives and a commercial ARTEX PRO edition remain. Researchers found more than 1,600 exposed consoles in early November.

The advisory links ARTEX to the October ConnectWise Cloud Backup breach. Microsoft attributed that campaign to China-aligned Storm-0940, which tried to authenticate against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.
key_points: The FBI says ARTEX-driven intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours in some cases.
ARTEX uses external LLMs such as Claude and GPT and survives in forks after its GitHub repo was removed.
The tool was used in the ConnectWise breach, where Huntress counted at least 162 compromised tenants.
